 What is PDRN Skincare? Why’Salmon DNA’ is Trending in Korean Beauty
 Salmon DNA is an unusual selling point for a face serum. Yet PDRN is now appearing across Korean beauty, from moisturisers to masks, with brands drawing on research that began in wound care. The ingredient has an intriguing scientific history, but the useful question for shoppers is what it can do in a product you apply at home.
 by 
 Ben Williams 
 2026-10-22 11:08 
 in 
 Beauty 
 Facebook Twitter Linkedin Email Whatsapp 
 What Is PDRN Skincare? 
 PDRN stands for polydeoxyribonucleotide: purified fragments of DNA traditionally sourced from salmon or trout. These fragments are processed for medical and cosmetic use; they aren’t raw fish material mixed into skincare.
 Researchers have studied PDRN in relation to tissue recovery and wound healing. Its move into serums and creams reflects growing interest in using those findings to develop products for skin appearance and texture.
 PDRN isn’t one fixed cosmetic formula. Brands can use different fragment sizes, concentrations and delivery systems, which can influence how a finished product behaves on the skin.
 Why Has Salmon DNA Become a Korean Beauty Trend? 
 The striking name helped PDRN attract attention, but its appeal goes beyond novelty. Unlike familiar ingredients marketed mainly for hydration or exfoliation, PDRN arrives with a research background in tissue repair.
 That doesn’t mean every cream is designed to repair skin in the medical sense. Across Korean skincare , DNA-derived ingredients now appear alongside familiar ingredients such as glycerin, niacinamide and peptides, each contributing to the product’s overall properties.
 What Does Research Say About PDRN? 
 Two 2026 publications help explain the interest, although they examined different uses of these materials:
 Clinical treatments: A review of seven randomised trials involving 183 people reported improvements in skin rejuvenation measures, scar outcomes and wound healing following polynucleotide or PDRN treatments. Findings for wound healing were particularly consistent, although the trials were relatively small and used differing treatment methods.
 Topical skincare: A PLOS ONE study compared a specially formulated 0.1% PDRN eye cream with a 0.1% retinol eye cream in 31 women. After four weeks, researchers reported improvements in wrinkle measurements and measures of skin thickness and density, with several results favouring the tested PDRN preparation.
 The eye-cream findings are encouraging, but their limitations matter. The study involved just 31 participants, lasted four weeks and tested one specific formulation around the eyes. Several authors were also affiliated with biotechnology companies, although the paper declared no competing interests.
 The researchers acknowledged that some early improvements could reflect hydration or skin plumping rather than lasting structural changes.
 -->
 These results support further investigation, rather than proving that PDRN skincare generally delivers similar benefits or performs better than retinol. Larger, independent studies would help establish how well topical PDRN works across different products and over longer periods.

 Is PDRN Serum the Same as Polynucleotide Injections? 
 No. Professional polynucleotide treatments deliver DNA-derived compounds into the skin, bypassing its protective outer layer. Serums and creams are applied to the surface, so fragment size and the formula carrying them influence how they behave.
 PDRN and polynucleotides are related, although preparations differ in their composition and intended use. An injected treatment and a facial serum should not be expected to give identical results.
 How Can You Identify PDRN on an Ingredient List? 
 You might not see the letters PDRN in a product’s ingredient list. Related materials often appear as Sodium DNA, Hydrolyzed DNA or Hydrolyzed Sodium DNA.
 For example, the PDRN Pink Peptide Serum within the Medicube skincare range combines Sodium DNA with ingredients including niacinamide, glycerin and peptides.
 The 2026 eye-cream trial did not test this Medicube serum, so its findings cannot be used as evidence of the serum’s effectiveness. 
 These ingredient names don’t always reveal the concentration or origin of the DNA. Traditional PDRN is commonly fish-derived, while some brands offer plant-based alternatives marketed as phyto-PDRN. These aren’t necessarily equivalent, making ingredient sourcing worth checking, particularly if you avoid animal-derived products or have fish allergies.
 What Should You Look for When Shopping? 
 Look beyond the words ‘salmon DNA’ on the packaging:
 Supporting ingredients: Glycerin and hyaluronic acid can add hydration, while niacinamide can help with uneven skin tone. Peptides have different functions depending on their type and formulation.
 Texture: A serum may layer easily beneath moisturiser; a richer cream may better suit dry skin.
 Ingredient source: Check whether the brand explains where its DNA-derived material comes from.
 Skin compatibility: Fragrance and other active ingredients may matter more than the headline ingredient if your skin is reactive.
 Is PDRN Skincare Worth Trying? 
 PDRN is an interesting ingredient to watch. Its research background offers reasons for curiosity, although evidence for the long-term benefits of everyday cosmetic products remains limited.
 If a PDRN product suits your skin and preferences, it may be worth trying. Just approach it as an emerging cosmetic ingredient rather than a proven shortcut to the results reported in clinical treatments.
